records.table: Glenfiddich 12 Year Old, from the distillery William Grant built in Dufftown, in Speyside, tastes of pear, butterscotch, cream and a little oak. Sherry and bourbon casks meet in marrying tuns before bottling, and it serves neat or long with soda.
records.story: William Grant (1839 to 1923) began building Glenfiddich in Dufftown in 1886 with the help of his nine children, seven sons and two daughters, and the first spirit ran from its copper stills on Christmas Day 1887. The name is Gaelic for the valley of the deer, which is why a stag stands on the label. The family firm, William Grant & Sons, passed from the founder to his sons and their descendants. For most of the twentieth century nearly all Scotch reached drinkers in blends, and in 1963 the firm began promoting Glenfiddich as a single malt beyond Scotland, in the triangular bottle that became its mark. In the 1950s the distillery took on its own coppersmiths and its own cooperage, a habit few distilleries kept. The 12 Year Old marries whisky from Oloroso sherry casks and bourbon casks in oak tuns before it is bottled. Many a guest new to Scotch names it first, and in its pear, butterscotch and malt it shows what a fruit-led Speysider tastes like.

records.table: The licence George Smith took out in 1824 in the glen of the River Livet stands behind The Glenlivet 12 Year Old, a gentle single malt of pineapple, pear, vanilla and toffee. European oak comes first and American oak after; sip it neat, or lengthen it with soda.
records.story: Before 1823 much of the whisky made in the glen of the Livet was distilled without a licence, and the name Glenlivet was already known for it. The Excise Act of 1823 made licensed distilling worth the trouble, and in 1824 George Smith (died 1871), a farmer at Upper Drumin, rode to Elgin and took out his licence: by the house's account the first legal distiller in the parish of Glenlivet. In the late 1850s the work moved down the hill to a larger distillery at Minmore. On his death in 1871 a son who had been training for the law came home to run the business. In 1884, as the house tells it, the son established the right to call his whisky The Glenlivet; other distilleries could add Glenlivet to their own names only as a hyphenated suffix, which is why old labels read Macallan-Glenlivet. In 1953 the firm merged with that of Glen Grant. The 12 Year Old is the soft, fruity Speyside benchmark, and the article on its label is a lesson in itself.

records.story: In 1824, soon after the Excise Act of 1823, a local farmer and schoolteacher took out a licence to distil on the Easter Elchies estate, on the high ground above the Spey near Craigellachie. Easter Elchies House, which dates from 1700, stands at the heart of the estate and is the house's emblem. In 1892 a wine merchant bought the distillery and renamed it Macallan-Glenlivet, borrowing the name of the famous glen to the south as many Speyside distilleries then did. His family kept it for about a century: shares went to outside companies from 1986, and in 1996 Highland Distillers bought the company, ending the family's hold. In 2018 a new distillery opened on the estate. The house sets out its way as Six Pillars, among them its curiously small stills and its sherry seasoned casks from Jerez. The dried fruit, the spice and the colour of the Sherry Oak 12 all come from the cask: it is the bottle that shows what sherry seasoned oak does to a Speyside malt.

records.story: Early in 1892 William Grant, whose Glenfiddich had first run in Dufftown in 1887, began to turn an eighteenth-century mansion beside it, Balvenie New House, into a second distillery. The work took fifteen months, and the first spirit ran on 1 May 1893, by one account from second-hand stills bought from Lagavulin on Islay and Glen Albyn in Inverness. Later the mansion was pulled down. Balvenie is one of the few Scotch distilleries that malts some of its own barley on a floor, by hand, with its own coppersmiths to tend the stills. In 1993 the distillery's malt master made DoubleWood: twelve years in American oak, then nine months in European oak sherry casks. It is often credited with bringing the idea of a cask finish to wide notice, and finishing has shaped the house's range in the years since. To explain a finish, pour it: the honeyed oak of the long years comes first, then the fruit the sherry casks added at the end.

records.table: Cask strength and Spanish oak butts that held Oloroso sherry define Aberlour A'bunadh, a Speyside single malt bottled in numbered batches: orange, cinnamon, dark chocolate and dried fruit. Start it neat, then add water slowly and taste again.
records.story: Aberlour's distillery was built in 1879 by James Fleming (1830 to 1895), a banker and grain merchant in the village; by some accounts an earlier distillery had worked nearby from 1826. Money he left founded the Fleming Cottage Hospital in Aberlour, opened in 1900. The story behind A'bunadh begins in the 1970s, when men at work on the still room are said to have found a bottle of old Aberlour hidden there, wrapped in a newspaper of 1898. They drank much of it, as the story goes, and what was left went to the laboratory, which set out to make a whisky in its style. The result came out in 1997: whisky from Oloroso sherry butts, bottled at the strength it left the cask, with no age statement and a batch number on each label. The name is Gaelic for of the origin. In October 2025 the house began a separate A'bunadh Sherry Cask Collection, finished in Oloroso and Pedro Ximénez casks, beside the numbered batches. One glass shows what cask strength means: taste it neat, then watch water open it.

bottle.label: Cask Strength replaced by Spanish Oloroso Sherry Butts, which a shop's photograph of the label shows and Wikipedia confirms; cask strength stays in the class, the table line and the card.
others: the A'bunadh Sherry Cask Collection added, so a guest who meets its bottle is not told it is the batch whisky.
open: story: the find is the house's legend and is told so; 1973 and 1975 are both given for it, so the record keeps the 1970s.
bottle.strength: about 59 to 62% rests on Wikipedia's batch table and shop listings (59.6 for the first batches, 61.6 for batch 81).
